query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Using an integrated approach that combines containerless electromagnetic levitation with ultrafast differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ high‐speed imaging along with CALPHAD-based simulations will allow accurate and efficient determination of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy specimens produced by conventional casting or powder-based methods with minimal contamination and homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the samples to containerless processing via electromagnetic levitation under an inert atmosphere while applying ultrafast DSC heating ramps and simultaneous high-speed optical imaging.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in a controlled high-purity inert gas environment (or high vacuum) to avoid heterogeneous nucleation; heating and cooling rates are optimized to minimize superheating/undercooling effects, with temperature calibration across the 1000–2000 °C range (typical for refractory HEAs).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a homogeneous, containerless liquid phase that prevents contamination and unwanted interfacial effects, while rapid transitions are captured by high-speed calorimetry and imaging.
generation.mechanism: Electromagnetic levitation eliminates contact with crucibles that can induce nucleation and contamination. Ultrafast DSC provides high resolution of the heat flow during the phase transition, while in situ imaging measures volume changes in real time. CALPHAD simulations help interpret the heat flow data by relating them to the underlying thermodynamic functions (enthalpy, entropy) and liquid structure, thereby reconciling experimental scattering in complex alloy composition space.
generation.predicted_outcome: The methodology is expected to yield melting temperatures within ±5 °C accuracy, enthalpy and entropy values with high quantitative fidelity, and volume change measurements with relative uncertainties of a few percent. This outcome will uniformly capture the fusion characteristics despite compositional complexity in the HEA family.
generation.baseline: Conventional DSC in contact with crucibles and slower heating rates often leads to errors from heterogeneous nucleation, contamination, and incomplete capturing of rapid liquid-phase transitions.
generation.boundary: The proposed approach applies primarily to HEAs that form homogeneous liquids without significant segregations or ongoing decomposition during melting. In alloys with severe microsegregation or sluggish phase reactions, additional corrections or alternative methods may be needed.
generation.uncertainty: The efficiency in high-throughput screening across varied compositions may be limited if unexpected phase segregation occurs upon melting. In addition, calibration of levitation and DSC signals for extremely high melting alloys still requires careful validation, so some experimental uncertainties could remain in quantitatively matching CALPHAD predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy alloys (across a range of compositions) using the standard casting method. Then, perform containerless electromagnetic levitation experiments coupled with ultrafast DSC and high-speed imaging under a tightly controlled inert atmosphere. Independently, measure the same thermodynamic properties using conventional (container-based) DSC with extensive calibration. Compare the melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy, and volume change data from both methods as well as against predictions from CALPHAD simulations.
measurements: Melting temperature (°C) from DSC peak onset
Enthalpy of fusion (J/g) derived from the integrated heat flow
Entropy of fusion calculated from enthalpy and melting temperature
Volume change at melting observed via high-speed imaging (using calibrated optical density changes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the containerless method does not provide melting temperature measurements within ±5 °C of the independent conventional method or if the integrated thermodynamic data (enthalpy, entropy, volume change) deviate by more than ±5% from both the conventional measurements and CALPHAD predictions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
